subject: Biotechnology
title: Xenotransplantation Ethics
description: A fast breakdown of Xenotransplantation Ethics for builders.

hook.text: Over 100,000 Americans wait for organ transplants — gene-edited pig organs could end the shortage. Should we use them?

buildup.text: In 2022, a pig heart was transplanted into David Bennett — the first gene-edited pig organ in a living human patient.

discovery.text: Ten gene edits removed pig antigens and added human immune compatibility genes — reducing rejection by the human body.

twist.text: Bennett survived two months before dying — his heart was infected with porcine cytomegalovirus, raising safety questions.

climax.text: Animal welfare groups argue gene-editing pigs as organ sources treats animals as mere spare parts — commodifying life.

punchline.text: Save a human life with a pig organ — xenotransplantation tests where we draw moral lines.

quiz.question: What went wrong with the first gene-edited pig heart transplant?
options: The human immune system immediately rejected the pig heart
The pig heart was infected with porcine cytomegalovirus, contributing to the patient's death two months later
The gene edits made the pig heart incompatible with human blood

details.summary: Xenotransplantation uses genetically modified animal organs, primarily from pigs, for human transplantation. Gene editing removes pig viruses and adds human compatibility genes, but raises ethical concerns about animal welfare, infection risk, and the boundary between species.
details.whyItMatters: Over 100,000 people await organ transplants in the US alone, and thousands die waiting. Xenotransplantation could eliminate organ shortage entirely, but requires resolving profound ethical questions about using animals as organ sources.
takeaways: Gene-edited pigs have organs compatible with the human immune system
Pig heart transplants into human patients began in clinical testing in 2022
Ethical concerns include animal welfare, zoonotic risk, and species boundaries

faq.question: Why are pigs used for xenotransplantation instead of primates?
faq.answer: Pigs are preferred because their organs are similar in size to humans, they breed quickly with large litters, and can be raised in controlled environments. Primate organs raise greater ethical concerns, higher zoonotic disease risk, and primates reproduce too slowly for organ supply.

faq.question: What is the risk of animal viruses infecting human recipients?
faq.answer: Porcine endogenous retroviruses embedded in pig DNA are the primary concern. Gene editing using CRISPR has successfully inactivated all 62 PERV sequences in donor pigs, and clinical monitoring of recipients has shown no evidence of PERV transmission to date.
